transcript.text: micrwave keeps tripping the eletric, not every time but like 1 in 3 when i press start, whole kitchen goes off. had to reset the fuse box 4 times today

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Please don't keep resetting the trip. Leave the appliance unplugged and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer before using it again. Please leave the microwave unplugged now and don't use it again until an engineer has checked it. A microwave that trips the house electrics is showing a real electrical fault, and it can get worse each time. The trip happens the moment you press start, which is when the microwave switches on its high-voltage heating circuit. 1. A breakdown in the high-voltage parts (the HV capacitor, HV diode or magnetron). This is the classic cause of tripping on start, and it is often intermittent at first.
2. A door interlock or monitor switch that is switching at the wrong moment. 3. Less likely, a damaged mains lead or plug, or the kitchen circuit already being heavily loaded when it trips. You can do these checks with it unplugged. 1. Look at the fuse box and see which switch has dropped. If it's the RCD (the switch with a test button), that points to earth leakage, usually a high-voltage part breaking down. If it's a single circuit breaker, that suggests a short or a heavy current draw.
2. Look along the mains lead and plug for scorch marks, melting or a cut sheath. Any of these means the lead or plug is part of the problem.
3. Open and close the door and see whether it shuts firmly and squarely, or feels loose or rattly. A sloppy catch makes the door switch suspect. All of these faults are inside the casing, and a microwave stores a lethal charge even when unplugged. Please don't open it; this is an engineer job. Be aware that a high-voltage fault on a cheaper microwave often costs more to repair than the microwave is worth. On a built-in or higher-end model, though, a repair is usually worthwhile. Which switch drops in the fuse box when it trips?
its the one that covers the kitchen sockets, the switch in the fuse box. sometimes theres a loud bang from inside the microwave when it goes too

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Stop using the microwave now: switch it off at the socket and unplug it, and don't run it again (not even empty) until we know why it sparked. Never take the outer casing off — parts inside can hold a lethal charge even when it is unplugged. That's a really useful answer, and the bang matters most. A breaker that drops the instant you press start, together with a loud bang from inside, means something in the high-voltage heating circuit is shorting out. That's a heavy fault current, not the slow leakage you'd expect from a damp or worn lead. Please keep it unplugged and don't use it again until an engineer has checked it. Most likely causes, in order:
1. A high-voltage component breaking down: the HV diode, HV capacitor or magnetron. These often fail intermittently at first, flashing over with a bang when the power hits them, which fits your 1 in 3. This is my leading suspect.
2. The door monitor switch. That can also trip the breaker on start. It's usually a click or pop rather than a bang, though.
3. Much less likely, the mains lead or plug. With a bang from inside the casing, it's unlikely to be the main cause. That isn't owner work on a microwave, so there's nothing more inside I'd ask you to check. One small point: some kitchen circuits are protected by an RCBO, a breaker with a small test button. That trips on both leakage and overload, so it doesn't change the picture here. Either way, the fault is in the microwave. The real question now is whether it's worth repairing. A diode or capacitor is a modest repair. A magnetron plus the call-out often costs more than a basic freestanding microwave is worth. On a built-in or combination model, a repair is usually worthwhile. Is yours built-in or freestanding, and roughly how old is it?
its freestanding, about 5 years old. russell hobbs one, silver. is it worth fixing or just bin it?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Honestly, for a five-year-old freestanding Russell Hobbs, I'd recycle it rather than repair it. These are budget machines, and repairs are rarely economic. The fault is internal, so an engineer has to diagnose and fix it. The call-out and diagnosis alone usually cost a fair chunk of a new microwave's price. 1. HV diode or capacitor (the more likely, cheaper end): the part is modest, but with labour the total still often comes close to a new basic microwave.
2. Magnetron: almost always costs more than the microwave is worth.
3. Door switch: a cheap part, but the labour is the same. Also, many engineers won't take on budget freestanding microwaves, and parts for some models can be hard to get. Whatever you decide, it mustn't be used again unless a qualified engineer has checked and repaired it. 1. Keep an eye on that kitchen breaker over the next day or two. If it stays on with everything else running normally, that suggests the microwave was the cause. If it still trips with the microwave out of the picture, get an electrician to look at the circuit.
2. Don't put it in the household bin. Take it to your local recycling centre's small electricals (WEEE) area, or use a retailer take-back scheme when you buy a new one. The only time I'd consider repair is if it's covered by an extended warranty or home appliance insurance, which is worth a quick check of your paperwork first.
